title: Who Is Harmanpreet Kaur? The Moga Batter Who Captained India to Its First Women's World Cup — and Just Became the First Female Cricketer Honoured With a Wax Statue
excerpt: Born in Moga, Punjab, Harmanpreet Kaur debuted for India at 20, announced herself with 171 not out in a World Cup semi-final, captained India in 211 internationals to its first Women's World Cup in 2025 — then stepped down in October 2026 and, weeks later, unveiled a wax statue in Jaipur organisers call the world's first of a female cricketer.
body:
• Harmanpreet Kaur Bhullar, 37, born in Moga, Punjab, captained India to its first Women's Cricket World Cup title on November 2, 2025, beating South Africa by 52 runs in the final at Navi Mumbai's DY Patil Stadium, according to her career record.
  • On October 6, 2026, she stepped down as India's captain across all formats after leading the side in 211 internationals, and continues as a player under her successor, Smriti Mandhana.
  • Her career numbers, as of October 28, 2026, stand at 388 internationals — 8 Tests, 167 one-day internationals and 213 T20 internationals — with 4,667 ODI runs and 4,438 T20I runs, and a record 331 runs in World Cup knockout matches.
  • On November 13, 2026, a wax statue of Harmanpreet was unveiled in Jaipur — a figure organisers describe as the world's first of a female cricketer. It will stand on permanent display at the 'Historica: Step into History' museum at Nahargarh Fort, alongside statues of Sachin Tendulkar and MS Dhoni, so readers visiting Jaipur can see it in person.

Two honours bookended Harmanpreet Kaur's autumn. On October 6, 2026, she gave up the India captaincy across Tests, one-day internationals and T20 internationals, ending a leadership run that had lasted, in its full-time form, a decade. Five weeks later, on November 13, she stood in Jaipur next to a wax statue of herself — a figure crafted by the Historica Museum that organisers say is the world's first wax statue of a female cricketer, unveiled at the Rajasthan International Centre and bound for permanent display at Nahargarh Fort, according to IANS. Between those two moments sits the achievement that defines her: on November 2, 2025, she captained India to its first Women's Cricket World Cup, taking the final catch herself as South Africa were dismissed in the final at Navi Mumbai.

"They are very great cricketers. I am still not at that level, but for me, it is a very big achievement that my statue is being made, and I'm sure that upcoming cricketers will get even more motivation from this."

— Harmanpreet Kaur, in Jaipur on November 13, 2026, on her statue standing alongside Sachin Tendulkar's and MS Dhoni's, as reported by CricTracker

A Moga childhood, 30 kilometres from the academy

Harmanpreet Kaur Bhullar was born on March 8, 1989, in Moga, Punjab, to Harmandar Singh Bhullar and Satwinder Kaur. Her father was a former sportsman who later worked as a clerk at a local judicial court; she has a younger sister, Hemjeet Kaur. She took to cricket after joining the Gian Jyoti School Academy, about 30 kilometres from her home, where she trained under Kamaldeesh Singh Sodhi and played with men during her formative years. In 2014 she moved to Mumbai and began working for the Indian Railways — the job that anchored many Indian women cricketers of her generation while the game itself paid little.

India came early. She made her one-day international debut at 20, against Pakistan at Bowral on March 7, 2009, during that year's World Cup, and her T20 international debut against England at Taunton that June. Her first ODI century came against England at Mumbai's Brabourne Stadium on February 3, 2013. The leadership thread started sooner than most remember: in 2012, with captain Mithali Raj and vice-captain Jhulan Goswami injured, the stand-in captain Harmanpreet led India past Pakistan in the Asia Cup final.

The 171 that changed the conversation

The innings that made her a household name arrived on July 20, 2017, in the World Cup semi-final against Australia at Derby: 171 not out off 115 balls, the highest individual score in a Women's World Cup knockout match and the highest by an Indian at a Women's World Cup. India won by 36 runs and reached the final, losing to England by nine runs at Lord's. At Jaipur this month, Harmanpreet herself identified that knock as the turning point, saying it played a pivotal role in transforming public perception of women's cricket in India, IANS reported.

The firsts accumulated. In 2016 she had already become the first Indian woman signed by an overseas T20 franchise, joining Sydney Thunder in Australia's Women's Big Bash League — a signing that put her in front of diaspora crowds in Australia years before franchise women's cricket existed at home. In November 2018 she became the first Indian woman to score a T20 international century, 103 off 51 balls against New Zealand. In 2019 she became the first Indian cricketer to play 100 T20 internationals, and in February 2023 the first Indian to pass 3,000 T20 international runs.

Captaincy: a decade of firsts in England and Australia

Harmanpreet first led India in a T20 international in 2012, became the full-time T20I captain in 2016, took the ODI captaincy after Mithali Raj's retirement in 2022, and became all-format captain in 2023, according to the Times of India's account of her stepping down. Her teams delivered a sequence of results Indian women's cricket had not produced before: a first bilateral ODI series win in England since 1999 in 2022, built around her own 143 not out, the highest score by an Indian captain in ODIs; a first Test victory over Australia, at Mumbai's Wankhede Stadium in December 2023; Commonwealth Games silver in Birmingham in 2022; Asian Games gold in 2022 and again in 2026; and a first T20I series win in England in July 2025. In all, she captained India in 211 internationals — 51 ODIs, of which India won 30, 155 T20 internationals, of which India won 92, and five Tests, of which India lost only one.

November 2, 2025: the World Cup itself

The defining tournament came at home. In the 2025 World Cup semi-final, India chased 339 against Australia — the highest successful chase in women's ODI history — with Harmanpreet scoring 89 in a 167-run partnership with Jemimah Rodrigues. In the final at the DY Patil Stadium on November 2, 2025, India beat South Africa by 52 runs, and Harmanpreet took the catch that dismissed Nadine de Klerk and ended the match. Her 20 runs in the final took her to 331 runs in World Cup knockout matches, a record. Speaking in Jaipur, she drew the comparison herself, as CricTracker reported: just as the men's 1983 World Cup win changed the landscape of men's cricket, she said, the women's title is now changing the landscape of the women's game — "and I'm sure this is just the beginning."

The franchise pioneer, at home and abroad

Harmanpreet's club career maps the professionalisation of the women's game. After Sydney Thunder came Melbourne Renegades, where she was named Player of the Tournament in the 2021–22 Big Bash after scoring 399 runs and taking 15 wickets in 11 matches, and stints with Manchester Originals and Trent Rockets in England's Hundred. At home she captained Supernovas to Women's T20 Challenge titles in 2018, 2019 and 2022. When the Women's Premier League finally launched, Mumbai Indians bought her for ₹1.80 crore at the inaugural auction in February 2023 and made her captain; she led them to the title that year and again in 2025, becoming the first captain to win multiple WPL trophies. For diaspora readers in Australia and England, she was often the first Indian woman cricketer they watched live, season after season, in their own leagues.

Stepping down, playing on

The end of the captaincy came after a BCCI review meeting in Guwahati attended by BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia, head coach Amol Muzumdar and her deputy Smriti Mandhana, the Times of India reported. Announcing the decision on Instagram on October 6, 2026, she wrote: "Today, I step down as captain of the Indian Women's Cricket Team across all formats." "Captaincy ends. The journey continues," she added — and it has: she played on as a batter in the October series against Zimbabwe, with Mandhana taking over as captain, as our coverage of the handover and of the Jaipur statue unveiling recorded.

The honours have kept pace with the cricket. She received the Arjuna Award in 2017. In 2023 she became the first Indian woman named among Wisden's Cricketers of the Year, and appeared in both the TIME100 Next list and the BBC's 100 Women list that year. In 2026 the Government of India awarded her the Padma Shri, the country's fourth-highest civilian honour. A reader who had never watched women's cricket can measure her from those facts alone: the Moga batter who trained 30 kilometres from home, played with the men because there was no other game available, and finished her captaincy as the third Indian — after Kapil Dev and MS Dhoni — to lift a Cricket World Cup, and the first woman to do it.
